entries.term: hit it out of the park
entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To do something extremely well, often much better than people expected.
entries.usage: Enthusiastic American praise, common at work, at school and in sports talk, often right after a presentation, performance or event: *You hit it out of the park!* Said about your own work it can sound boastful, so it's mostly used to praise others. *Knock it out of the park* is just as common, and *it* can be replaced by the task: *She hit that interview out of the park.*
entries.pattern: hit / knock it (or the task) out of the park
examples: Your presentation was amazing — you really **hit it out of the park** today.
The caterer **hit it out of the park**; our guests are still talking about the brisket.
In his first Broadway role, the young actor **hit it out of the park**.

drill.sentence: My sister was nervous about her wedding toast, but she hit it {{out of the park}} — half the room was in tears.
drill.hint: brilliantly, like a home run

entries.related: *knock it out of the park* — same meaning; *nail it* — do something perfectly, very common; *a home run* — a big success (noun).
entries.origin: From baseball, where hitting the ball out of the stadium is a home run.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To annoy or irritate someone, usually through your manner or attitude rather than one specific action, and often without meaning to.
entries.usage: Common in conversation about coworkers, neighbors and first impressions: *He just rubs me the wrong way.* It's milder than *really annoy* and often admits that the dislike is hard to explain. British English usually says *rub someone up the wrong way*.
examples: I can't explain it, but something about the new neighbor **rubs me the wrong way**.
His habit of finishing other people's sentences **rubbed** a lot of coworkers **the wrong way**.
The new owner's comments about 'lazy' local fans **rubbed** a lot of people in town **the wrong way**.

drill.sentence: There's nothing really wrong with my best friend's new boyfriend, but his know-it-all attitude {{rubs me the wrong way}}.
drill.hint: irritates me, more through his manner than any single act (not *gets on my nerves*)

entries.related: *get on someone's nerves* — annoy someone, often by repeated behavior; *ruffle someone's feathers* — upset someone, usually by challenging them; *grate on someone* — irritate slowly over time.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To upset or annoy some people, usually by challenging them or by changing the usual way of doing things.
entries.usage: Common at work, in politics and in organizations, about someone who makes changes or speaks bluntly. It often sounds half-approving, as if the trouble was worth it: *She ruffled some feathers, but she got results.* Variants include *ruffle a few feathers* and *ruffle someone's feathers*.
entries.pattern: ruffle some / a few / someone's feathers
examples: The new principal **ruffled some feathers** when she canceled the annual talent show.
I know my comments at the budget meeting **ruffled some feathers**, but someone had to say it.
Grandma **ruffled a few feathers** at Thanksgiving by asking my cousins when they were finally getting married.

drill.sentence: If you want to change how the homeowners' association works, you're going to {{ruffle some feathers}}.
drill.hint: upset a few people — a bird image (not *step on toes*)

entries.related: *step on someone's toes* — offend someone by entering their area of responsibility; *rock the boat* — cause trouble by challenging how things are; *rub someone the wrong way* — irritate through your manner.
entries.origin: From birds, which fluff up their feathers when they are angry or disturbed.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To learn the basic procedures and practical knowledge you need in a new job, place or activity.
entries.usage: Used about new employees, students, volunteers and other newcomers, often as *still learning the ropes* or *it takes time to learn the ropes*. The related *show someone the ropes* means to teach a newcomer, and *know the ropes* means to be experienced. It's friendly and neutral, so it fits both work and casual talk.
entries.pattern: learn / know the ropes; show someone the ropes
examples: I'm still **learning the ropes**, so please be patient if I ask a lot of questions.
It took me a few months to **learn the ropes** as a volunteer firefighter.
Our new postdoc **learned the ropes** quickly and was running the microscope on her own within weeks.

drill.sentence: My dad joined a community theater at sixty-five, and the younger actors helped him {{learn the ropes}}.
drill.hint: pick up the basic procedures as a newcomer (not *get the hang of it*)

entries.related: *show someone the ropes* — teach a newcomer; *get the hang of something* — learn how to do one specific task; *a fish out of water* — someone who feels out of place in a new setting.
entries.origin: From sailing ships, where new sailors had to learn which rope controlled which sail.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: In a risky position where one more mistake could get you into serious trouble, often with someone in authority.
entries.usage: Usually *be on thin ice* or *skate on thin ice*, often with *already* and *with* + person: *You're already on thin ice with your boss.* It's a common warning from parents, teachers and managers. It can also describe a weak legal position: *The company is on thin ice legally.*
entries.pattern: be / skate on thin ice (with someone)
examples: After missing two deadlines, Jake is **on thin ice** with his manager.
You're already **on thin ice** for breaking curfew, so don't push it.
After two failed inspections, the restaurant is already **on thin ice** with the health department.

drill.sentence: My landlord has warned me twice about noise, so I'm {{on thin ice}} — one more complaint and I'm out.
drill.hint: in a risky spot where one more problem means real trouble (a frozen-lake image)

entries.related: *in hot water* — already in trouble; *on borrowed time* — likely to end soon; *walk on eggshells* — act very carefully so you don't upset someone.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: Completely unexpected, strange, or unrelated to what came before.
entries.usage: Common in American conversation and journalism, usually as *come out of left field*: *That question came out of left field.* It describes surprising events, questions and ideas, and it's neutral rather than critical. Don't confuse it with *(way) out in left field*, which describes a person or idea as strange or badly wrong.
entries.pattern: come out of left field; a bit out of left field
examples: My dad's decision to sell the house and buy a sailboat came completely **out of left field**.
That suggestion is a little **out of left field**, but I kind of like it.
The layoffs came **out of left field**; the company had just reported record profits.

drill.sentence: We were talking about dinner plans when my roommate asked, completely {{out of left field}}, whether I believe in ghosts.
drill.hint: unexpectedly — a baseball image (not *out of the blue*)

entries.related: *out of the blue* — suddenly, without warning; *out of nowhere* — very similar and neutral; *off the wall* — strange in a crazy or funny way.
entries.origin: From baseball; why *left* field in particular is still debated.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: A fact, idea or clue that draws attention away from the real issue, either by accident or on purpose.
entries.usage: Common in debates, journalism and mystery stories, where a false clue is a classic plot device. In an argument, calling a point *a red herring* is a criticism: it says the point is irrelevant and distracts from the real question. Typical patterns are *be a red herring* and *turn out to be a red herring*.
examples: The muddy boots turned out to be **a red herring**; the real killer never left the house.
Critics say the fight over the new logo is **a red herring** that distracts from the budget cuts.
We spent two days chasing a memory leak that was just **a red herring**; the real bug was in the config file.

drill.sentence: The mechanic said the rattling noise was {{a red herring}}; the real problem was a leaking brake line.
drill.hint: something misleading that pulls attention from the real cause (a fish image)

entries.related: *a smoke screen* — something used on purpose to hide the truth; *a wild-goose chase* — a long, useless search; *beside the point* — irrelevant.
entries.origin: Usually traced to an 1807 story by the English journalist William Cobbett about using a smoked herring to lead hunting dogs off a hare's trail.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To aim for success over a long period, accepting slow progress or small losses now instead of going for quick wins.
entries.usage: Common in business, politics, careers, investing and sports commentary, usually as approval and often in the progressive: *She's playing the long game.* It contrasts with *quick wins* and *short-term gains*. *A long game* also works as a noun phrase: *Investing is a long game.*
examples: He turned down the bigger salary because he's **playing the long game** and wants to learn from the best.
Index-fund investors **play the long game** and ignore the daily ups and downs of the market.
The coach is **playing the long game**, giving young players minutes even if it costs a few wins this season.

drill.sentence: Instead of selling her paintings cheaply now, Ana is {{playing the long game}} and slowly building a name with galleries.
drill.hint: aiming for success years from now instead of quick gains (a strategy image)

entries.related: *in it for the long haul* — committed for a long time; *short-termism* — focus on quick results, critical; *a marathon, not a sprint* — a long effort that needs steady pacing.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: A situation in which competitors keep lowering prices, wages, taxes or standards to beat each other, so that almost everyone ends up worse off.
entries.usage: Common in economics, politics and business journalism, and almost always critical. Typical topics are corporate taxes, wages, labor and environmental rules, and prices. Frequent patterns are *a race to the bottom on* + topic and *start* or *trigger a race to the bottom*.
examples: Countries keep cutting corporate taxes to attract companies, and critics call it **a race to the bottom**.
Budget airlines seem to be in **a race to the bottom** when it comes to legroom.
Some freelance websites turn design work into **a race to the bottom**, with people offering logos for five dollars.

drill.sentence: When every delivery app slashes driver pay to beat the others, the result is {{a race to the bottom}}.
drill.hint: a contest where everyone keeps lowering standards (not *a price war*)

entries.related: *a price war* — competitors cutting prices; *a downward spiral* — a situation that keeps getting worse; *a zero-sum game* — one side's gain is the other's loss.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: A situation in which one side's gain is exactly the other side's loss, so both cannot win at the same time.
entries.usage: Common in politics, business and everyday arguments, most often in the negative to reject competitive thinking: *Trade isn't a zero-sum game.* *Zero-sum* also works as an adjective: *zero-sum thinking*. It sounds analytical and fits both writing and speech.
examples: Office politics can feel like **a zero-sum game**: if your coworker gets the promotion, you don't.
Some parents treat youth sports as **a zero-sum game**, as if every minute another kid plays is a minute stolen from theirs.
With three teenagers and one bathroom, mornings in our house are **a zero-sum game**.

drill.sentence: Love isn't {{a zero-sum game}}; loving your new baby doesn't mean you love your older child any less.
drill.hint: a situation where one side wins only what the other loses (an economics term)

entries.related: *win-win* — good for both sides, the opposite; *dog-eat-dog* — fiercely competitive; *a race to the bottom* — competition that keeps lowering standards.
entries.origin: From game theory, where it names a game in which the players' gains and losses add up to zero.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To continue in its natural way until it ends by itself, without anyone stopping or changing it.
entries.usage: Used for illnesses, trends, relationships and crises, often as *let it run its course*; *has run its course* means something is finished or no longer useful. It sounds calm and accepting, sometimes resigned. The possessive follows the subject: *the protests ran their course*.
entries.pattern: let something run its course; has run its course
examples: There's no cure for a cold; you just have to let it **run its course**.
I think our friendship has **run its course**; we don't have much in common anymore.
Most fashion trends **run their course** within a few years and then come back decades later.

drill.sentence: After six seasons, the show had clearly {{run its course}}, and the network quietly canceled it.
drill.hint: reached its natural end, with nothing new to offer (not *run out of steam*)

entries.related: *fizzle out* — end gradually and disappointingly; *run out of steam* — lose energy before finishing; *have had its day* — be no longer popular or useful.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: The most important question in a situation, which nobody can answer yet.
entries.usage: Very common in conversation, interviews and news commentary, either as a reply to a hard question (*That's the million-dollar question*) or to introduce one: *The million-dollar question is whether …* It sounds light and a little playful. *The $64,000 question* is an older version.
examples: Will the new stadium actually bring in tourists? That's **the million-dollar question**.
**The million-dollar question** is whether the drug works as well in older patients.
Fans keep asking **the million-dollar question**: will she ever tour again?

drill.sentence: Everyone agrees the team needs a new coach, but who would actually take the job is {{the million-dollar question}}.
drill.hint: the crucial unknown that everyone wants answered (a prize-money image)

entries.related: *the $64,000 question* — older, same meaning; *anybody's guess* — impossible to know; *the burning question* — an urgent question many people want answered.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: A situation that nobody has experienced before, so there are no rules or past examples to guide you.
entries.usage: Common in news, business and science, often as *in uncharted territory* or *enter uncharted territory*. It can sound worried (record debt, a new kind of crisis) or excited (a new technology, a new stage of life). *Uncharted waters* means the same.
entries.pattern: be in / enter / move into uncharted territory
examples: With prices this high, the housing market is in **uncharted territory**.
Raising twins was **uncharted territory** for both of us, but we figured it out.
Models this large put us in **uncharted territory**; nobody knows exactly how they'll behave.

drill.sentence: None of us had ever cared for a parent with dementia, so we were in {{uncharted territory}}.
drill.hint: a situation no one has been through, like land not yet on any map

entries.related: *uncharted waters* — same meaning, sea image; *break new ground* — do something for the first time; *unprecedented* — never happened before, more formal.

entries.term: a canary in the coal mine
entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: Something whose early trouble warns of a larger danger that may soon affect others.
entries.usage: Common in journalism and in writing about economics, health and the environment. It often takes *the* instead of *a*, and *for* + what is threatened: *the canary in the coal mine for the economy*. It sounds serious and is used to call for attention or action.
examples: Rising credit card defaults may be **a canary in the coal mine** for the wider economy.
Frogs are often called **the canary in the coal mine** because they react so quickly to pollution.
Looking back, my constant headaches were **the canary in the coal mine**; I was heading for burnout.

drill.sentence: When the smallest shops on Main Street started closing, it was {{a canary in the coal mine}} for the whole downtown.
drill.hint: an early warning of bigger danger — a bird image (not *a red flag*)

entries.related: *a red flag* — a warning sign of a problem; *a harbinger* — formal, a sign of something to come; *the writing is on the wall* — clear signs of coming failure.
entries.origin: Coal miners once took canaries underground; if the bird got sick or died, it warned them of toxic gas.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To try to convince people who already agree with you.
entries.usage: Very common in American conversation, often as a friendly reply: *You're preaching to the choir* means 'I already agree with you.' It also criticizes speeches, ads or campaigns that only reach existing supporters. British English often says *preach to the converted*.
examples: 'Taxes are way too complicated.' 'You're **preaching to the choir**; I spent all weekend on mine.'
The museum's ad campaign mostly **preached to the choir** and didn't bring in many new visitors.
Telling a room full of nurses that hospitals are understaffed is **preaching to the choir**.

drill.sentence: You don't need to convince me that this city needs better buses — you're {{preaching to the choir}}.
drill.hint: talking to someone who already agrees (the American church version)

entries.related: *preach to the converted* — same meaning, more common in British English; *an echo chamber* — a group that only hears views it already shares.

entries.term: hold someone's feet to the fire
entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To keep putting pressure on someone, especially a leader or organization, so that they keep a promise or take action.
entries.usage: Common in politics, journalism and activism, about voters, reporters or watchdog groups pressing officials: *We'll hold their feet to the fire.* It sounds determined and approves of the pressure. *Keep someone's feet to the fire* is a less common variant.
entries.pattern: hold someone's feet to the fire (on something)
examples: Local reporters **held the mayor's feet to the fire** until she released the full budget.
The union promised to **hold management's feet to the fire** on the new safety rules.
My workout buddy **holds my feet to the fire**; if I skip the gym, she texts me until I show up.

drill.sentence: The school board promised a new playground, and the parents plan to {{hold their feet to the fire}} until it's built.
drill.hint: keep pressing them to keep their word (a heat image)

entries.related: *hold someone accountable* — plainer and more formal; *keep the pressure on* — keep pushing; *breathe down someone's neck* — watch someone too closely.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To watch someone too closely, especially while they work, so that they feel pressured or annoyed.
entries.usage: Almost always a complaint, typically in the progressive: *My boss is always breathing down my neck.* It's used about bosses, parents, coaches and investors who check on someone too often. The possessive changes with the person: *breathing down her neck*, *down our necks*.
examples: I can't concentrate with my manager **breathing down my neck** every five minutes.
My mom kept **breathing down my neck** while I filled out my college applications.
Investors are **breathing down the CEO's neck** after three bad quarters in a row.

drill.sentence: I'll finish the dishes faster if you stop {{breathing down my neck}} and let me do it my way.
drill.hint: watching me too closely (not *hovering*)

entries.related: *micromanage* — control every small detail of someone's work; *hover* — stay close and watch; *look over someone's shoulder* — watch what someone is doing.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To make a situation, issue or debate more confusing or less clear, often by adding irrelevant or conflicting information.
entries.usage: Common in politics, law, news and serious discussion. It is often critical, suggesting that someone confuses things on purpose to avoid blame, but it can be neutral when new facts make a question less clear. The plural *waters* is the usual form.
examples: The company's lawyers tried to **muddy the waters** by blaming a supplier.
Conflicting advice from friends only **muddied the waters** when I was choosing a college.
A new study with the opposite result has **muddied the waters** on whether coffee is good for you.

drill.sentence: The neighbors had almost settled the fence dispute until a third neighbor {{muddied the waters}} with an old survey showing a different property line.
drill.hint: made the issue less clear — a pond image (not *clouded the issue*)

entries.related: *cloud the issue* — make a question harder to judge; *a red herring* — a distraction from the real issue; *clear the air* — ease tension by talking openly.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To get yourself, through your own decisions, into a difficult situation with no good way out.
entries.usage: Used in politics, negotiations, planning and personal life, especially about promises or statements that limit your options later. The reflexive pronoun changes with the subject: *painted himself / ourselves into a corner*. It suggests poor planning rather than bad luck.
entries.pattern: paint yourself / himself / itself / ourselves into a corner
examples: By promising customers free shipping forever, the little online shop **painted itself into a corner**.
Don't tell the kids the trip is definite, or you'll **paint yourself into a corner** if it falls through.
We **painted ourselves into a corner** by hard-coding the file paths everywhere.

drill.sentence: Sam told everyone he'd run the marathon in under three hours, and now he's {{painted himself into a corner}}.
drill.hint: got stuck because of his own choices — a home-improvement image (not *boxed in*)

entries.related: *box yourself in* — limit your own options; *back someone into a corner* — force someone into a hard position; *shoot yourself in the foot* — harm yourself through a mistake.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To deal calmly with a problem, criticism or change, without letting it upset you or stop you.
entries.usage: Usually praise, often with *just* or *seem to*: *She took the news in stride.* The object goes between *take* and *in stride*, and it is often *it*. British English says *take something in your stride*.
entries.pattern: take it / the news / the criticism in stride
examples: Our flight was canceled, but the kids **took it in stride** and played cards at the gate.
The rookie **took the boos in stride** and scored twice in the second half.
She **took the criticism in stride** and rewrote the proposal over the weekend.

drill.sentence: When the moving truck showed up six hours late, my grandmother just {{took it in stride}} and made everyone sandwiches.
drill.hint: handled it calmly (not *rolled with it*)

entries.related: *roll with the punches* — adapt to problems as they come; *keep your cool* — stay calm; *shrug something off* — treat something as unimportant.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To meet every requirement or expectation on a list, so that something seems ideal or at least acceptable.
entries.usage: Common at work and in talk about hiring, shopping, housing and dating, as in *the apartment checks all the boxes*. It can be positive, or slightly critical when meeting the list is not enough: *He checks all the boxes, but I'm not excited*. British English says *tick all the boxes*.
examples: The house **checks all the boxes**: three bedrooms, a big yard and a short commute.
The candidate **checked all the boxes** in the interview, but something felt off.
My mom keeps trying to set me up with guys who **check all the boxes** on her list.

drill.sentence: We visited six schools, and only one {{checked all the boxes}}: small classes, a good music program and a short bus ride.
drill.hint: met every item on our list (the American form; not *fit the bill*)

entries.related: *tick all the boxes* — British version; *fit the bill* — be suitable for a purpose; *a check-the-box exercise* — something done only to meet formal rules, critical.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: The detailed conditions of a contract or offer, often in small type, which are easy to miss and may contain limits or extra costs.
entries.usage: Used about contracts, warranties, insurance, loans and special offers, as in *read the fine print* or *buried in the fine print*. It usually carries a warning that the real terms are less attractive than the headline. British English usually says *the small print*.
examples: Always read **the fine print** before you sign a lease.
The 'free' trial had a forty-dollar cancellation fee hidden in **the fine print**.
The new law looks generous, but **the fine print** excludes most part-time workers.

drill.sentence: The airline advertised flights to Hawaii for ninety-nine dollars, but {{the fine print}} said the price only applied on Tuesdays in February.
drill.hint: the detailed conditions in tiny type (the American form)

entries.related: *the small print* — British version; *strings attached* — hidden conditions, as in *no strings attached*; *a catch* — a hidden problem in an offer.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: Work it out yourself from the facts; the conclusion is obvious. Speakers use it to point to a conclusion without saying it directly.
entries.usage: Common in American conversation, usually as an imperative, often *You do the math.* It typically hints at something negative or ironic that the speaker doesn't want to say outright. It can also simply mean to calculate, and the word *math* marks it as American.
examples: He's been 'working late' every night and comes home smelling like someone else's perfume. **You do the math**.
**Do the math**: if your rent goes up 20 percent and your salary doesn't, you're getting poorer.
'Why did they cancel the show?' '**Do the math** — every episode cost ten million dollars, and nobody was watching.'

drill.sentence: The stadium cost two billion dollars and seats only thirty thousand people. {{Do the math}} — the city will never get its money back.
drill.hint: work it out from the numbers yourself (an arithmetic phrase)

entries.related: *connect the dots* — see how separate facts fit together; *it doesn't add up* — something seems wrong or illogical; *figure it out* — plainer.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: The basic practical details of how something works or is done, as opposed to the general ideas.
entries.usage: Common at work and in teaching, in the pattern *the nuts and bolts of* + activity. It also works as an adjective with hyphens: *a nuts-and-bolts guide*. It's slightly informal and often contrasts with theory or big-picture talk.
entries.pattern: the nuts and bolts of + activity
examples: The workshop skips the theory and goes straight to **the nuts and bolts** of starting a small business.
My first job at a coffee shop taught me **the nuts and bolts** of customer service.
The two companies have agreed to merge; now the lawyers have to work out **the nuts and bolts**.

drill.sentence: I understand the idea behind composting; I just need someone to explain {{the nuts and bolts}} — what goes in and how often to turn it.
drill.hint: the practical details (a hardware image; not *the basics*)

entries.related: *the nitty-gritty* — the most important practical details; *the ins and outs* — all the details of a complex matter; *the big picture* — the overall view.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: Extra features that make a product or system more attractive but are not necessary for its main purpose.
entries.usage: Common about phones, cars, software, houses and events. It can be neutral (*with all the bells and whistles* = fully equipped) or critical when the extras hide a weak basic product. Typical patterns are *all the bells and whistles*, *no bells and whistles* and *without the bells and whistles*.
examples: I don't need a phone with all the **bells and whistles**; I just want a good camera and a long battery life.
The cheapest version of the car has no **bells and whistles**, but it's reliable.
Their wedding had all the **bells and whistles**: a string quartet, fireworks and a taco truck.

drill.sentence: My dad's new grill has a Wi-Fi thermometer, a rotisserie and all the other {{bells and whistles}} he could find.
drill.hint: fancy optional features (a noise-making image)

entries.related: *frills* — unnecessary extras, as in *no-frills*; *gimmicks* — tricks to attract attention; *the nuts and bolts* — the basic working parts.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: The largest part of something, often more than a fair share.
entries.usage: Common in news, business and everyday talk about money, time, work or credit, almost always as *the lion's share of* + noun. Most people use it simply to mean "most," but it often hints that the share is unfairly large.
examples: My older brother always got **the lion's share** of our parents' attention.
**The lion's share** of the city's budget goes to schools and road repairs.
In many small cities, one or two airlines control **the lion's share** of flights.

drill.sentence: My roommate and I are supposed to split the cooking, but honestly she does {{the lion's share}} of it.
drill.hint: by far the biggest part (an animal image; not *the bulk*)

entries.related: *the bulk of* — most of, neutral; *the majority of* — more than half, more formal; *a drop in the bucket* — a tiny amount.
entries.origin: From Aesop's fable in which a lion hunts with other animals and then keeps all the prey for himself.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: An amount that is far too small to make a real difference compared with what is needed.
entries.usage: Common in news and conversation about money, donations, aid and pollution, often followed by *compared to* or *for* + who: *a drop in the bucket for a city this size*. It sounds realistic rather than insulting. British English usually says *a drop in the ocean*.
examples: A ten-million-dollar donation sounds generous, but for a company that size, it's **a drop in the bucket**.
Skipping my daily latte saves money, but it's **a drop in the bucket** next to my student loans.
One country cutting emissions is **a drop in the bucket** if the biggest polluters don't follow.

drill.sentence: I donated twenty dollars to the hospital fundraiser, which I know is just {{a drop in the bucket}}.
drill.hint: a tiny amount compared to what's needed (the American form)

entries.related: *a drop in the ocean* — British version; *a fraction* — a small part; *the lion's share* — the largest part.
entries.origin: Often traced to the King James Bible (Isaiah 40:15): *the nations are as a drop of a bucket*.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To pay a very high price for something, often the highest price in the market.
entries.usage: Common in conversation, ads and business news, with *for* + item or *to* + verb. It's neutral about whether the price is fair and usually signals high demand or high quality. The seller's side is *get top dollar*: *We got top dollar for the house*.
entries.pattern: pay top dollar for something / to do something
examples: Collectors will **pay top dollar** for a mint-condition Michael Jordan rookie card.
We **paid top dollar** for front-row seats, and the band played for only forty minutes.
Tech companies **pay top dollar** for engineers with AI experience.

drill.sentence: Families {{pay top dollar}} to live in this school district, so even a small condo costs a fortune.
drill.hint: accept the highest prices on the market (not *spend a fortune*)

entries.related: *pay through the nose* — pay much too much, as a complaint; *get top dollar* — sell at a high price; *pay a premium* — pay extra for something special.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: Good value for the money or effort that you spend.
entries.usage: Very common in American speech, ads and reviews, often as *more bang for your buck* or *the most bang for your buck*. The pronoun can change (*bang for our buck*), and *bang for the buck* is also common. It's casual; in formal writing, use *value for money* or *cost-effective*.
entries.pattern: more / the most bang for your buck
examples: If you want the most **bang for your buck**, shop at the farmers market right before it closes.
A used Honda gives you a lot more **bang for your buck** than a new luxury car.
Cleaning up the data gave us more **bang for our buck** than tuning the model ever did.

drill.sentence: Our travel agent says Portugal gives you the most {{bang for your buck}} in Western Europe right now.
drill.hint: value for the money you spend (casual American slang)

entries.related: *value for money* — standard phrase, more common in British English; *cost-effective* — formal; *pay top dollar* — pay a very high price.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: A product, business or activity that reliably brings in a lot of money, often far more than it costs to run.
entries.usage: Common in business news and office talk. It can be neutral (*the company's cash cow*) or critical, suggesting that someone squeezes money out of people: *Critics say the state treats tolls as a cash cow*. The verb *milk* often goes with it.
examples: For most movie theaters, popcorn is **a cash cow**; it costs pennies to make and sells for eight dollars.
The printer is cheap, but the ink cartridges are the company's real **cash cow**.
Critics say the city treats speed cameras as **a cash cow** rather than a safety tool.

drill.sentence: The neighborhood bake sale became such {{a cash cow}} that the school now holds one every month.
drill.hint: a dependable money-maker (a farm-animal image)

entries.related: *a gold mine* — a source of great wealth or value; *milk something* — take as much money from it as possible; *a money pit* — something that keeps costing money, the opposite.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To spend all of your income on regular costs, so that you have no savings and depend on each paycheck to pay your bills.
entries.usage: Common in American news, surveys and talk about personal finance, often with *even* or *still*: *Millions of families live paycheck to paycheck*. It's sympathetic and describes financial pressure more than bad money habits. *Paycheck* is the American word for a salary payment.
examples: Even with two jobs, my parents were **living paycheck to paycheck** when I was a kid.
When you **live paycheck to paycheck**, one car repair can turn into a crisis.
Surveys suggest that many middle-class households **live paycheck to paycheck**, even with good jobs.

drill.sentence: After rent, daycare and student loans, the young couple had nothing left at the end of the month; they were {{living paycheck to paycheck}}.
drill.hint: spending everything they earned before the next payday

entries.related: *live hand to mouth* — have barely enough to survive; *make ends meet* — earn just enough to pay for basics; *a nest egg* — savings for the future.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To go beyond the usual limits of what is done or thought possible, by trying something new or risky.
entries.usage: Used about technology, art, fashion, comedy and sports, usually as praise for innovation. It can also mean going a little too far: *The show pushes the envelope on what's acceptable on network TV*. *Envelope-pushing* works as an adjective.
examples: The chef likes to **push the envelope** with dishes like squid-ink ice cream.
The late-night host **pushed the envelope** so far that the network got hundreds of complaints.
Car makers keep **pushing the envelope** on how far an electric car can go on one charge.

drill.sentence: The designer's new collection really {{pushes the envelope}}, with dresses made entirely of recycled plastic.
drill.hint: goes beyond the usual limits (an aviation phrase; not *breaks the mold*)

entries.related: *break new ground* — do something for the first time; *think outside the box* — think creatively; *cross the line* — go beyond what is acceptable.
entries.origin: From aviation, where the *flight envelope* is the safe performance limit of an aircraft; Tom Wolfe's *The Right Stuff* (1979) made the phrase popular.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To find and point out weaknesses or mistakes in an argument, plan, theory or story.
entries.usage: Common at work, in law and politics, and in everyday arguments; *poke a hole in* is also used. It can be hostile (*the defense poked holes in his story*) or helpful, as when you invite it: *Go ahead and poke holes in it*. British speakers more often say *pick holes in*.
entries.pattern: poke holes / a hole in + argument, plan, story
examples: The defense attorney **poked holes in** the witness's story until the jury doubted all of it.
Before we pitch this to the client, I want you to **poke holes in** it.
My teenage son loves to **poke holes in** every rule I make.

drill.sentence: Every time I explain my plan to quit my job and travel, my dad finds a way to {{poke holes in}} it.
drill.hint: find the weak spots in (not the British *pick*)

entries.related: *pick holes in* — same, more common in British English; *shoot down* — reject an idea completely; *play devil's advocate* — argue the other side to test an idea.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: A quick, temporary fix that hides a problem for a while but does not solve its real cause.
entries.usage: Always critical, and common in politics, business and IT: *a Band-Aid solution to a deep problem*. *Band-Aid* is a brand name for small adhesive bandages, so it's capitalized; people also say *a Band-Aid fix* or just *a Band-Aid*. British English often says *a sticking plaster*.
examples: Raising bus fares is **a Band-Aid solution**; the transit system needs steady long-term funding.
A bucket under the leak is **a Band-Aid solution**; sooner or later we'll need a new roof.
Restarting the server every night is **a Band-Aid solution**; we still don't know why it crashes.

drill.sentence: Giving the overworked nurses free pizza on Fridays is {{a Band-Aid solution}}; what they really need is more staff.
drill.hint: a quick fix that hides the real problem — a first-aid image (not *a stopgap*)

entries.related: *a stopgap* — a temporary measure until a real one is ready, more neutral; *a quick fix* — fast but shallow; *paper over the cracks* — hide problems instead of fixing them.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: Complete freedom to act, spend or decide as you wish, without limits or oversight.
entries.usage: Common in politics, business and family talk, usually in the negative: *We're not giving the contractor a blank check.* Typical verbs are *give*, *hand*, *write* and *get*. British English spells the word with a *-que* ending.
examples: The city council refused to write the builders **a blank check** and capped the project at forty million dollars.
My parents paid for college, but that didn't mean I had **a blank check** for spring break.
The new CEO was handed **a blank check** to restructure the company however she liked.

drill.sentence: Grandpa told us to order whatever we wanted, but that wasn't {{a blank check}} to order the lobster.
drill.hint: unlimited freedom to spend (a banking image; not *a free pass*)

entries.related: *carte blanche* — full freedom to act, more formal; *a free hand* — freedom to act without interference; *a free pass* — permission to avoid rules or criticism.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: A final, desperate attempt to prevent failure or defeat when almost all hope is gone.
entries.usage: Very common in news and sports reporting: *a last-ditch effort to save the deal*. The usual pattern is *a last-ditch effort / attempt / bid to* + verb. It stresses urgency, and the attempt often fails.
entries.pattern: a last-ditch effort / attempt / bid to + verb
examples: In **a last-ditch effort** to save their marriage, they rented a cabin in Vermont for a week, just the two of them.
Negotiators made **a last-ditch effort** to avoid a strike before the midnight deadline.
The team's **last-ditch effort**, a long pass with two seconds left, fell short.

drill.sentence: The night before the trip, I made {{a last-ditch effort}} to convince my cousin to come with us.
drill.hint: a final, desperate attempt (a trench image)

entries.related: *a Hail Mary* — a desperate attempt with little chance, American; *as a last resort* — when everything else has failed; *at the eleventh hour* — at the last possible moment.
entries.origin: From the old military phrase *die in the last ditch*, meaning fight to the death in the last line of defense.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: Something that has already been agreed or decided and cannot be changed now.
entries.usage: Common in business, politics and conversation, often in the negative: *It's not a done deal yet*. It can suggest that people had no chance to object: *The decision was a done deal before the meeting even started*.
examples: Don't celebrate yet; the merger isn't **a done deal** until regulators approve it.
By the time residents heard about the new highway, it was already **a done deal**.
'Are you really moving to Denver?' 'Yep, it's **a done deal** — we signed the lease yesterday.'

drill.sentence: We wanted a say in the new playground design, but the parks department treated it as {{a done deal}}.
drill.hint: something already settled that can't be changed (not *a fait accompli*)

entries.related: *a fait accompli* — a decision already carried out before others could react, formal; *set in stone* — fixed and impossible to change; *seal the deal* — make an agreement final.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To finalize an agreement, or to do the last thing that makes a success certain.
entries.usage: Common in sales, sports, dating and politics. The subject is often the thing that persuades: *The view sealed the deal*. It sounds positive and casual; formal writing prefers *conclude* or *finalize an agreement*.
examples: The house was great, but the big backyard **sealed the deal** for us.
A goal in the eighty-ninth minute **sealed the deal** for the home team.
The salesman offered free winter tires to **seal the deal**.

drill.sentence: I was unsure about adopting the puppy until he fell asleep in my lap — that {{sealed the deal}}.
drill.hint: made my decision certain (not *clinched it*)

entries.related: *clinch the deal* — same meaning, common in sports and sales; *close the deal* — complete a sale; *a done deal* — already decided.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To increase the stakes, demands or risks in a situation, often to put more pressure on someone.
entries.usage: Common in politics, business, sports and conflicts: *Both sides keep upping the ante*. *Up* is a verb here, so the forms are *upped* and *upping the ante*. *Raise the ante* means the same.
examples: The union **upped the ante** by threatening a nationwide strike.
My neighbors put up a giant inflatable Santa, so this year I'm **upping the ante** with a full light show.
Streaming services keep **upping the ante** with bigger budgets for their original shows.

drill.sentence: My coworker offered to bet ten dollars on the game, and then our boss {{upped the ante}} to fifty.
drill.hint: a poker phrase: he made the bet bigger (not *raised the stakes*)

entries.related: *raise the stakes* — same meaning; *escalate* — make a conflict more serious, formal; *double down* — commit even more strongly to a risky position.
entries.origin: From poker, where the ante is the stake each player puts in before the cards are dealt.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: A complete disaster or chaotic failure, such as an event, a project or a person's life, that is often painful to watch.
entries.usage: Common in American conversation and media criticism: *The launch was a train wreck*. It's harsh and often humorous, and calling a person *a total train wreck* is quite insulting. *Like watching a train wreck* stresses that you can't look away.
examples: The first rehearsal was **a train wreck**; nobody knew their lines and the lights kept failing.
The live TV interview turned into **a train wreck** when the actor forgot which movie he was promoting.
My first attempt at Thanksgiving dinner was **a train wreck**: burned turkey, raw stuffing and a screaming smoke alarm.

drill.sentence: Our road trip was {{a train wreck}} from start to finish: a flat tire, a lost wallet and three days of rain.
drill.hint: a complete mess (a railroad image; not *a disaster*)

entries.related: *a disaster* — neutral; *a dumpster fire* — slang, a hopelessly chaotic situation; *a car crash* — British, used in a similar way, as in *car-crash TV*.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To claim or suggest that someone said or meant something that they did not say or mean.
entries.usage: Mostly used in arguments and interviews as a defense: *You're putting words in my mouth*. It's common in debates, politics and relationships when someone twists what was said. *Put words into someone's mouth* is also correct.
examples: I never said the plan was bad — the article **put words in my mouth**.
The interviewer kept **putting words in the coach's mouth**, so he stopped answering.
Let your sister answer for herself; stop **putting words in her mouth**.

drill.sentence: I said I was tired, not that I didn't want to see you. Please don't {{put words in my mouth}}.
drill.hint: claim I said things I never said (a body-part image)

entries.related: *twist someone's words* — change the meaning of what someone said; *take something out of context* — quote only part so the meaning changes; *a straw man* — a weaker version of an argument, easy to attack.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: A small problem or setback that slows progress for a short time but does not stop it.
entries.usage: Common in business, politics and personal life, often to reassure people: *This is only a bump in the road*. Because it plays down a problem, critics may say a serious issue is *more than a bump in the road*. The plural *bumps in the road* is common for a series of small setbacks.
examples: Losing our biggest client hurt, but it was just **a bump in the road**.
Every marriage hits a few **bumps in the road**, and ours is no exception.
My doctor called the one high blood-sugar reading **a bump in the road**, not a reason to panic.

drill.sentence: Failing my driving test the first time was just {{a bump in the road}}; I passed easily a month later.
drill.hint: a small, temporary setback, like an uneven spot on a highway (not *a hiccup*)

entries.related: *a setback* — neutral, big or small; *a hiccup* — a small, brief problem; *hit a snag* — run into an unexpected problem.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To be suddenly abandoned, or to stop applying completely, usually because circumstances have changed.
entries.usage: Common in conversation about plans, rules, diets and habits, often in the past tense. Typical subjects are *plans*, *rules*, *routines*, *manners* and *logic*: *Logic goes out the window when people panic*. *Out the window* is the American form; British speakers often say *out of the window*.
examples: Once the kids got sick, our vacation plans **went out the window**.
My diet **goes out the window** whenever my mom makes lasagna.
During the pandemic, a lot of the old rules about working from home **went out the window**.

drill.sentence: We'd agreed to stay calm at dinner, but that {{went out the window}} the moment Uncle Joe brought up politics.
drill.hint: was suddenly abandoned — an image of throwing something out of the house

entries.related: *fall by the wayside* — be abandoned gradually; *go down the drain* — be wasted; *be thrown out* — be rejected.

entries.term: pull the rug out from under someone
entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To suddenly take away support, help or a promise that someone was relying on, leaving them in a difficult position.
entries.usage: Common about funding, jobs, deals and relationships, and always critical of the person who does it. The passive *have the rug pulled out from under you* is very common, and *pull the rug from under someone* is a shorter variant. It stresses surprise as well as loss.
examples: Two weeks before the season started, the sponsor **pulled the rug out from under** the team.
Cutting the program's funding in the middle of the year **pulled the rug out from under** hundreds of students.
When the landlord sold the building, we **had the rug pulled out from under us** with only a month's notice.

drill.sentence: I'd planned the whole move around my brother's truck, and then he {{pulled the rug out from under}} me by canceling the night before.
drill.hint: suddenly took away the support I was counting on (a floor-covering image)

entries.related: *leave someone in the lurch* — abandon someone in a difficult situation; *let someone down* — disappoint someone; *move the goalposts* — change the rules after something has started.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: A long list of items, such as problems, complaints, demands or tasks, often presented one after another.
entries.usage: Common in journalism, politics and work talk, in the pattern *a laundry list of* + plural noun. It's often mildly critical, suggesting that the list is long, unsorted or boring. Typical nouns after it are *complaints*, *demands*, *problems* and *side effects*.
entries.pattern: a laundry list of + plural noun
examples: The inspector handed us **a laundry list** of problems with the house.
The union came to the table with **a laundry list** of demands.
The drug ad ends with **a laundry list** of side effects read at top speed.

drill.sentence: Before every trip, my dad gives us {{a laundry list}} of things to check: locks, stove, windows and lights.
drill.hint: a long series of items — a household-chores image (not *a checklist*)

entries.related: *a litany* — a long, repetitive list, often of complaints, formal; *a wish list* — things you would like to have; *a to-do list* — tasks you need to do.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To have several different roles or responsibilities at the same time, especially in a job.
entries.usage: Common about startups, small businesses, nonprofits and family life, and frequent in job ads and interviews. It's neutral or positive, suggesting flexibility. Variants include *wear a lot of hats*, *wear multiple hats* and *wear two hats*.
examples: At a five-person startup, you have to **wear many hats**: sales, support and sometimes cleaning the kitchen.
As a single dad, I **wear many hats** — cook, driver, tutor and referee.
Our school librarian **wears many hats**, from running the chess club to fixing the printers.

drill.sentence: As the oldest of six kids, Maria had to {{wear many hats}} growing up: babysitter, cook and homework helper.
drill.hint: take on several different roles (a clothing image)

entries.related: *a jack of all trades* — a person who can do many different jobs; *juggle* — manage several tasks at once; *spread yourself too thin* — take on too much.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To finish the small remaining tasks or details so that something is complete.
entries.usage: Common before a deadline, a vacation, a move or the end of a job: *Let me tie up a few loose ends first*. It sounds organized and calm. Don't confuse it with *at loose ends* (American) or *at a loose end* (British), which mean having nothing to do.
examples: I'm taking Friday off to **tie up some loose ends** before the baby arrives.
I spent my last week at the company **tying up loose ends** on two unfinished projects.
The final episode **tied up all the loose ends**, so fans finally learned who the father was.

drill.sentence: Before we move to Chicago, we need to {{tie up loose ends}} here: cancel the gym membership, sell the couch and return the neighbor's ladder.
drill.hint: finish the small remaining tasks (a string image)

entries.related: *wrap up* — finish something; *dot the i's and cross the t's* — take care of every small detail; *at loose ends* — American, having nothing to do.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: In a very weak or dangerous state, so that something could fail or end at any moment.
entries.usage: Used in news and conversation about lives, careers, governments, deals and relationships: *His career is hanging by a thread*. It usually follows *be*, often in the progressive, and it sounds dramatic and serious.
examples: After the car accident, his life was **hanging by a thread** for two days.
The peace talks are **hanging by a thread** after last night's attack.
Our little bookstore was **hanging by a thread** until a viral video brought in new customers.

drill.sentence: Their marriage was {{hanging by a thread}} when they finally agreed to see a counselor.
drill.hint: very close to ending — a sewing image (not *on the rocks*)

entries.related: *on the rocks* — of a relationship, in serious trouble; *on its last legs* — about to fail or stop working; *touch and go* — uncertain, especially about survival.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To stop a problem or bad habit at an early stage, before it can grow into something serious.
entries.usage: Common with parents, teachers, managers and doctors, usually as *nip it in the bud*; the object comes between *nip* and *in the bud*. It sounds decisive and practical. Some native speakers say *nip it in the butt* by mistake, but the word is *bud*, as on a plant.
entries.pattern: nip it / the problem in the bud
examples: If your puppy starts chewing shoes, **nip it in the bud** right away.
The manager **nipped the gossip in the bud** by talking to the whole team directly.
City inspectors hope the new traps will **nip the rat problem in the bud** before summer.

drill.sentence: My son started lying about his homework, so we sat him down to {{nip it in the bud}} before it became a habit.
drill.hint: stop it early (a gardening image)

entries.related: *head something off* — prevent something before it happens; *stamp out* — end something completely, often by force; *stop something in its tracks* — stop it suddenly.
entries.origin: From gardening: pinching off a bud stops it from growing into a flower or fruit.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: Said when little time is left to act or to finish something, and the pressure is growing.
entries.usage: Used in news, sports, politics and everyday life, often as a warning. Typical patterns are *the clock is ticking on* + task and *the clock is ticking for* + person. It's a full clause, so it usually stands alone or comes after a dash or colon.
examples: **The clock is ticking** for the rescue teams, who have about three days to find survivors under the rubble.
Come on, **the clock is ticking** — the store closes in fifteen minutes!
If you want those cheap flights, **the clock is ticking**: the sale ends Sunday.

drill.sentence: The passport office takes about six weeks, and we leave in eight, so {{the clock is ticking}}.
drill.hint: time is running short (a timepiece image; not *time's running out*)

entries.related: *time is running out* — plainer; *against the clock* — racing to finish before a deadline; *down to the wire* — until the very last moment.
